## Definition

A **variable** is anything that can vary or take on different values. In research, variables are the characteristics or properties we measure, manipulate, or control.

## Types of Variables in Experiments

| Variable Type | Definition | Role |
|--------------|------------|------|
| Independent (IV) | Manipulated by researcher | Presumed cause |
| Dependent (DV) | Measured outcome | Presumed effect |
| Extraneous | Uncontrolled variables | Potential noise |
| Confounding | Varies systematically with IV | Threatens validity |

## Examples

| Research Question | IV | DV |
|-------------------|----|----|
| Does caffeine improve memory? | Caffeine (yes/no) | Memory score |
| Does music affect concentration? | Music type (none/classical/pop) | Task accuracy |
| Does sleep duration affect mood? | Hours of sleep | Mood rating |

## Variable vs. Constant

| Variable | Constant |
|----------|----------|
| Changes across conditions/participants | Kept the same |
| Source of variation we study | Controlled to reduce noise |
| Example: Drug dosage | Example: Room temperature |

## Operationalising Variables

Variables must be **operationalised** - defined in terms of how they are measured or manipulated:

| Abstract Concept | Operationalised As |
|------------------|-------------------|
| Intelligence | Score on IQ test |
| Stress | Cortisol level in saliva |
| Happiness | Rating on 1-10 scale |
| Attention | Reaction time on task |

## DataLab Connection

At each DataLab station, identify the IV (what differs between conditions) and the DV (what is measured). For example, at the **Reflex Test**, the IV is stimulus type and the DV is reaction time.
